newsitem.title: USA: Rubin tells IMF U.S. on guard against inflation.
newsitem.headline: Rubin tells IMF U.S. on guard against inflation.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reassured the International Monetary Fund on Sunday that the United States would be on the alert against the risk of higher inflation.
"I can assure you we will be on guard against a resurgence in inflation,' Rubin said in a speech to the IMF's policy-making Interim Committee.

Questions about the U.S. commitment to fighting inflation have arisen following the Federal Reserve's decision last week to keep interest rates unchanged. The IMF itself has called for higher U.S. interest rates to keep inflation here in check.
"The united States is currently enjoying an extraordinary period of balanced non-inflationary growth," Rubin said.
He reiterated the Clinton administration's commitment to balancing its budget and welcomed the progress made by many European nations in reducing their deficits.

"While the outlook for sustained economic growth across the globe has improved, we still face many macroeconomic challenges," Rubin said. "In the industrialized countries, we must ensure that the economic expansion solidifies and strengthens."
Europe continues to be saddled with high rates of unemployment, highlighting the importance of structural economic reforms to spur job creation, Rubin said.

He welcomed the multilateral plan to provide debt relief to poor nations and reiterated U.S. support for the sale of modest amount of IMF gold to help finance the Fund's participation in the initiative.
"The sale of a modest amount of gold ... is a reasonable and prudent step," he said.
Rubin called it "unrealistic and counterproductive" to rely solely on bilateral contributions to finance its participation in the debt relief program.

"We, therefore, welcome the indication by the Managing Director (Michel Camdessus) that there is the necessary majority for a decision, as the need arises, to sell up to five million ounces of gold," Rubin said.

The Treasury chief though seem less enamored with Camdessus's proposal for a selective issue of 26 billion Special Drawing Rughts to IMF member nations. "While the United States is prepared to be pragmatic, we must be careful to avoid excessive allocations," he said.
